name: libaegis (AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-128X/256X)
baseline: AES-256-GCM (SUPERCOP aes256gcmv1; on this host the fastest implementation is Romain Dolbeau's VAES code; the OpenSSL wrapper 'opensslnew' is also measured and is slower)
workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP AEAD 'long+0 encrypt' benchmark: cycles/byte for long messages with no associated data, computed as 1/1920 of the cycle-count difference between a 2048-byte and a 128-byte message (not 1536-byte messages)
claimed_speedup: long+0 encrypt quartiles on hertz: aegis128l 0.18/0.19/0.19 cycles/byte vs aes256gcmv1 0.55/0.56/0.57 cycles/byte, about 2.9-3x faster (derived from page data). 1536+1536 encrypt: aegis128l 0.20-0.21 vs aes256gcmv1 0.55-0.56. The wider AEGIS-128X4 variant (also in libaegis) measures 0.07-0.08 cycles/byte long+0, about 7-8x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: From the eBACS web-impl pages (SUPERCOP 20260831, hertz). Fastest aegis128l implementation 'aesnib': clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall. Fastest aes256gcmv1 implementation 'dolbeau/vaesenc-int': clang -march=native -Os -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall.
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (Raptor Lake); AMD EPYC 7543; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, AVX-512+VAES) — single core, 16 KB messages
stars_or_usage: 146 stars; AEGIS is now published as RFC 10032 (linked from the libaegis README) and is also shipped inside libsodium
tradeoffs: The X2/X4 speedups require VAES/AVX-512 or equivalent wide vector-AES instructions; on CPUs without vector-AES, plain AEGIS-128L/256 is as fast or faster than the X-variants. AEGIS has a shorter cryptanalytic track record than AES-GCM (in active study since 2013).
caveats: eBACS measures SUPERCOP's own AEGIS implementations, not libaegis. The winning aegis128l code on hertz is 'aesnib' (no author credited); Frank Denis's sodium-aesni (libsodium) scores close behind, and the aegis128x2/x4 code in SUPERCOP is credited to Frank Denis. The aes256gcmv1 row is the best of several AES-GCM implementations. On hertz that is dolbeau/vaesenc-int. The OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew) is slower in the web-impl selection-time column: about 5764 for opensslnew vs 3258 for dolbeau and 1241 for aegis128l aesnib, so the gap against OpenSSL itself is likely larger than 3x. Compiler and flags ARE disclosed on the per-machine web-impl pages. libaegis's own README chart (img/bench-encryption.png, first-party, 16 KB encryption) does state its CPUs. On AMD Zen 4 with turbo off: aegis128l 208.44 Gb/s vs aes256-gcm (BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s. On Apple M1: 114.61 vs 41.6 Gb/s. The chart's baseline is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL, and the libaegis benchmark.zig does not include AES-GCM.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos aead cipher c++ (surfaced aegis-aead/libaegis); corroborated via bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-hertz.html
IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/523 'Adding more parallelism to the AEGIS authenticated encryption algorithms'

verification.tier_reason: eBACS/SUPERCOP is a well-known independent suite. On the hertz page (Ryzen 7 7700) aegis128l runs at 0.18-0.19 cycles/byte and aes256gcmv1 at 0.55-0.57. The public harness and web-impl pages give compiler, flags and CPU, but the measured aegis128l code (the uncredited 'aesnib' implementation) is not shown to be libaegis. The fastest AES-GCM is also Dolbeau's VAES code, not OpenSSL, so this is B, not A.
verification.notes: The numbers are accurate and belong to the aegis128l and aes256gcmv1 rows. The workload wrongly said 1536-byte messages; 'long' is the 2048-vs-128-byte differential. The record's caveats wrongly said compiler flags were undisclosed and the README charts had no CPU, and both are corrected. Tier would be A for the AEGIS algorithm vs OpenSSL AES-GCM, but the measured code is not shown to be libaegis's.

name: HiAE (High-throughput Authenticated Encryption)
workload: Single-core AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput across 14 named ARM and x86 CPUs (server/desktop/laptop/mobile/router), message sizes 64B-16384B, -O3 builds, vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CTR, SNOW-V-GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S and AEGIS-128L.
claimed_speedup: AEAD at 16384 B (Table 10): 340.02 Gbps (HiAE) vs 51.90 Gbps (OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM) on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (~6.6x, derived from page data); 171.46 vs 36.49 Gbps on Intel Xeon W9-3495X (~4.7x, derived from page data); 253.19 vs 38.80 Gbps on AMD EPYC 9334 (~6.5x, derived from page data). The abstract states over 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM in AEAD mode, 'making it the fastest AEAD solution on ARM chips and setting a new performance record on the latest x86 processors'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4 (x86 servers/desktop, Ubuntu 22.04 or WSL2), GCC 10.3 (Kunpeng/openEuler), GCC 14 (Apple M-series), ArkCompiler 3.0.0.5 (Huawei mobile), openWRT GCC 11.2.0 (router); -O3 maximum optimization used for every implementation compared
hardware: 14 CPUs in Table 9/10: Intel Xeon W9-3495X, AMD EPYC 9334, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon Gold 6326, Intel Core i7-11700, Intel Xeon Gold 6242R, Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, HiSilicon Kunpeng 920, Kunpeng 920X, Kirin 9000S, Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen1, Apple M2 Max, Apple M3 Pro, Rockchip RK3568 (an M1 MacBook Air is named in the setup text but has no result row)
tradeoffs: Reference repo carries no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused/redistributed as-is. HiAE is a brand-new (2025) design with far less cryptanalysis history than AES-GCM or even AEGIS; the paper's own results show HiAE falls slightly behind Rocca on older Xeon Gold 6242R/E5-2620 v3 CPUs that lack VAES.
caveats: Very new design (2025) by the paper's authors; numbers are first-party, from a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The public repo harness (test/performance_test.c) benchmarks HiAE only; the OpenSSL comparison code is not published. On mobile phones the AES-256 baseline was hand-implemented rather than OpenSSL. HiAE trails Rocca on pre-VAES Xeons (Gold 6242R, E5-2620 v3). Under active cryptanalysis: ePrint 2025/1180 'Cryptanalysis of the Authenticated Stream Cipher HiAE' (now a minor revision of a ToSC 2026 paper), 2025/1203 'Analyze the Security of the AEAD Scheme HiAE by Algebraic Techniques', and the designers' rebuttal 2025/1235. The reference repo has no license file; an MIT-licensed implementation exists at hiae-aead/libhiae (59 stars), but its README does not benchmark against AES-GCM.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=HiAE: https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/377 'HiAE: A High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption Algorithm for Cross-Platform Efficiency'

verification.tier_reason: ePrint 2025/377 Table 10 does compare HiAE against OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on 14 named CPUs with GCC version and -O3 stated, but the paper is a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the designers (ePrint lists 'Publication info: Preprint'; no venue found on Crossref), and the public harness (test/performance_test.c) times only HiAE with no OpenSSL/baseline code, so it is neither A (baseline benchmark code not public) nor B (not peer-reviewed/independent).
verification.notes: All three quoted numbers match Table 10 exactly; the only fix is marking the ratios as derived (7950X is 6.55x, not 6.5x). Metadata checked: no LICENSE file, not archived or a fork, 21 stars, last commit 2025-11-11 (active). Orchestrator may prefer hiae-aead/libhiae (MIT) as the copyable repo, but that is a different project URL, so I did not change repo_url.

name: SNOW-V-GCM
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput vs input size (64B-16384B) on a laptop CPU; SNOW-V-GCM implemented in C++ with AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ intrinsics, benchmarked using code extracted from OpenSSL's own benchmarking harness against OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev (2019-04-01) AES-256-GCM assembly.
claimed_speedup: Table 3, AEAD, 16384 B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM C++) vs 34.42 Gbps (OpenSSL AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster (derived from page data). Roughly even at 2048 B (30.71 vs 30.49); AES-256-GCM wins at 1024 B and below (e.g. 64 B: 8.54 vs 5.16 Gbps).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 + NASM, 'most possible optimizations switched on', native x64 build
hardware: Intel Core i7-8650U @1.90GHz (Turbo up to 4.20GHz), single thread
stars_or_usage: SNOW-V is a 3GPP/ETSI candidate stream cipher for 5G; no widely used, independently maintained open-source repo of SNOW-V-GCM was located in this search
tradeoffs: Only faster than OpenSSL AES-256-GCM for larger messages (roughly >=4KB); for short messages (<2KB) OpenSSL's hand-tuned, instruction-stitched assembly wins outright. The paper's own C++ implementation does not get GHASH "for free" the way OpenSSL's asm does.
caveats: Single 2018-era ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev, 2019-04-01); the win is small (~13%) and only above ~2 KB. The paper prints the SNOW-V AVX2 keystream code and a portable SNOW-V-GCM reference, but not the PCLMULQDQ-optimized GCM build or the harness that produced Table 3. Counter-evidence: HiAE (ePrint 2025/377, Table 10) measured the official SNOW-V-GCM implementation well below OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on every modern x86 CPU tested (e.g. 19.92 vs 51.90 Gbps on Ryzen 9 7950X, 13.04 vs 36.49 Gbps on Xeon W9-3495X at 16 KB). No maintained public repo, so usability is 'reference'.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=SNOW-V: https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1143 'A new SNOW stream cipher called SNOW-V'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (ePrint 2018/1143, published by the IACR in FSE 2020). Table 3 shows SNOW-V-GCM beating OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev AES-256-GCM asm at 16 KB on a named i7-8650U. It falls short of A: compiler flags are only 'most possible optimizations switched on', the benchmark harness adapted from OpenSSL is not published, and the benchmarked AVX2/PCLMULQDQ SNOW-V-GCM build is not printed (Appendix D has a portable GHASH reference, and Appendix E has AVX2 code only for the SNOW-V keystream).
verification.notes: Numbers and setup (VS2017 + NASM, i7-8650U, single thread) match the paper exactly. The tier drops from A to B because neither the flags nor the benchmarked code/harness are public. Consider flagging this entry, because a later third-party measurement (the HiAE paper) contradicts the speed win on current CPUs.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 16384B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM) vs 34.42 Gbps (AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster. Advantage shrinks with message size and reverses below ~2048B (e.g. at 64B, AES-256-GCM wins: 8.54 Gbps vs 5.16 Gbps).
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmarked on a single, now-old (2018-era) ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev); no maintained public repo found, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable' even though full source is printed in the paper's appendix.

name: Bitsliced AEGIS-128L / AEGIS-128X2 (constant-time, no-AES-NI platforms)
workload: Single-core, 16 KB message AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput on ARM/RISC-V CPUs lacking AES instructions and on WebAssembly, plus ARM Cortex-M4 cycle counts, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM from OpenSSL 3.3 (on Cortex-A53) and BoringSSL (elsewhere); also a pure-TypeScript benchmark on Apple M5 Max/Bun vs the noble-ciphers pure-JS AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 2, 16 KB messages, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM: ARM Cortex-A53 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (OpenSSL 3.3), 1.6x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V 193 (128L) / 333 (128X2) vs 137 Mb/s (BoringSSL), 1.4-2.4x; SiFive U74 182 / 311 vs 130 Mb/s, 1.4-2.4x; WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host 2241 / 2912 vs 480 Mb/s, 4.7-6.1x. Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 (fixsliced AES-128-GCM, protected GHASH) and 208 (unprotected table AES-128-GCM). Table 3, pure TypeScript on Apple M5 Max/Bun, 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (noble AES-128-GCM, 1.8x) and 256 MB/s (noble ChaCha20-Poly1305, 1.3x).
hardware: ARM Cortex-A53 (64-bit); SpacemiT X60 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); SiFive U74 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host; ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller; Apple M5 Max (pure TypeScript under Bun)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars (aegis-aead/aegis-bitsliced); companion pure-TypeScript port jedisct1/js-aegis-aead (MIT, 4 stars) used for the JS numbers
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for platforms lacking AES/vector-AES instructions (microcontrollers, RISC-V without crypto extensions, WASM, plain JS). On hardware with AES-NI/VAES, hardware-accelerated AEGIS or the AEGIS-X modes (see separate entry) are faster than this bitsliced code.
caveats: Published 2026-06/07 as a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the implementation's author; not yet independently reproduced. The C/Zig benchmark harness (src/test/benchmark.zig) measures only AEGIS variants; the baseline AES-GCM runs are not part of the published code, and compilers/flags are unstated. The repo README currently shows different, higher WebAssembly figures (AEGIS-128X2 3154, AEGIS-128L 3429 Mb/s) than the paper (2912 / 2241 Mb/s). The JS comparison uses the companion repo jedisct1/js-aegis-aead, whose 'bun run bench' does include noble-ciphers, but that baseline is not the listed OpenSSL/BoringSSL one.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1338 'Bitslicing the AEGIS'

GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file is plain MIT (Frank Denis, based on Adomnicai's work). name: Rocca (AES-based AEAD for 6G)
workload: Single-thread throughput in encryption-only and AEAD modes, messages 64B to 16384B, 13-byte associated data. AEAD mode repeats init, AD, encryption, tag and finalization for every message. Rocca, SNOW-V, Tiaoxin-346 and AEGIS (from SUPERCOP) were built into OpenSSL (latest PDF says 3.1.0-dev; the Jan 2022 revision says 3.0.0-alpha3-Dev) and compared with OpenSSL's AES-256-GCM/CTR/CBC, ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305, and SNOW-V-GCM.
claimed_speedup: 16384B AEAD on i7-1068NG7 (Table 7): Rocca 150.95 Gbps vs OpenSSL AES-256-GCM 29.08 Gbps (~5.2x, derived from page data) and vs ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps (~19.9x, derived from page data). The paper text says 4.16x faster than SNOW-V and 3.10x faster than AES-256-CTR at 16384B; both figures come from the encryption-only rows. The lead shrinks on other CPUs and for small messages. On the i9-11900 (Appendix A, Table 9), 16384B AEAD is 175.12 vs AES-256-GCM 117.60 Gbps (~1.5x, derived from page data), and Rocca is slower than AES-256-GCM at 256B (13.81 vs 15.57 Gbps) and at 64B (3.68 vs 4.51 Gbps). These numbers are for the revised Rocca (key feedforward in initialization). The original peer-reviewed ToSC 2021 paper reports 138.22 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 30.59 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.57 Gbps at 16384B AEAD.
hardware: Main table (Table 7): Intel Core i7-1068NG7 @2.30GHz, 32GB RAM. Appendix A adds Intel i9-12900K, i9-11900 and i9-10910 (Windows 10 Pro / macOS Big Sur 11.4), plus ARM NEON builds on Apple M1, Apple A15 Bionic and Qualcomm Snapdragon 888.
license: CC BY (license of the ePrint 2022/116 paper; the reference implementation exists only in the paper's Appendix C)
stars_or_usage: Peer-reviewed in IACR ToSC 2021(2) (presented at FSE 2022). ePrint 2022/116 is the full version: 4 revisions, last on 2023-03-16. The only standalone code found is a third-party C implementation of the original Rocca, ericlagergren/rocca (BSD-3-Clause, 5 stars, last commit 2022-01-28, no benchmarks). The successor Rocca-S has separate implementations such as jedisct1/zig-rocca-s (MIT, 21 stars).
tradeoffs: The original Rocca was later shown to have practical forgery/committing weaknesses (see IACR ePrint 2024/901 and the ToSC 2024/2025 Derbez et al. and Takeuchi et al. papers) and was superseded by the redesigned Rocca-S. Treat these numbers as a data point on the AES-NI+SIMD 'wide round function' technique, not as a currently-recommended cipher.
caveats: The numbers at benchmark_url (the latest ePrint PDF, 2023-03-16) are for the REVISED Rocca, which adds key feedforward in initialization after the Hosoyamada et al. ToSC 2022(3) attack: a full 256-bit key recovery with about 2^128 data and time, which breaks the original 256-bit claim. They are not for the original design. The original design's peer-reviewed numbers are in ToSC 2021(2): 138.22 vs 30.59 / 7.57 Gbps. Across ePrint revisions the OpenSSL baseline numbers stay identical to two decimals (AES-256-GCM 29.08 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps on the i7; 57.87 and 21.99 on the i9-12900K) while the OpenSSL version label and the Rocca numbers change. So the baselines were probably not re-measured. Compiler and flags are never stated. The advantage depends heavily on the CPU: only about 1.5x over AES-256-GCM on the i9-11900, and Rocca loses at 64B and 256B there. The code is C with AES-NI/NEON intrinsics, not C++. The design has since been superseded by Rocca-S.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=Rocca AES-based encryption beyond 5G: https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/116 'Rocca: An Efficient AES-based Encryption Scheme for Beyond 5G (Full version)'

verification.tier_reason: Table 7 of ePrint 2022/116 compares Rocca, built into OpenSSL, with OpenSSL AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 on a named CPU (i7-1068NG7). ePrint 2022/116 is the full version and a major revision of the peer-reviewed ToSC 2021(2) paper, and that paper shows the same win (138.22 vs 30.59 Gbps). Tier A is impossible: the benchmark harness is not public and neither version states a compiler or flags. The only code is the reference C in Appendix C.
verification.notes: The record's name says 'original/pre-attack', but the numbers it cites (150.95 Gbps, OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev) belong to the revised Rocca in the 2023 ePrint revision. Either rename the entry to 'Rocca (revised, key feedforward)' or repoint benchmark_url to the ToSC 2021 paper (https://tosc.iacr.org/index.php/ToSC/article/download/8904/8480) and use its original-design numbers. The record's language field says C++, but the code is C. repo_url could point to ericlagergren/rocca (original Rocca, BSD-3-Clause), but that repo has no benchmarks.

name: Intel(R) Multi-Buffer Crypto for IPsec (intel-ipsec-mb)
baseline: OpenSSL (AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput) and FreeBSD OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) default kernel crypto (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 VPN throughput)
workload: Raw AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput vs OpenSSL on an AVX2 host, plus end-to-end iperf3 VPN throughput (OpenVPN DCO, IPsec-ESP, WireGuard) in pfSense/FreeBSD with an IIMB-based engine replacing OCF as the in-kernel crypto provider
claimed_speedup: Netgate AsiaBSDCon 2023 paper: on an AVX2 test host, IPsec-MB did 18.1 Gbps AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 on 1400-byte blocks vs OpenSSL's maximum of 10.4 Gbps on 16 kB blocks, about 1.7x (derived from page data). In pfSense/FreeBSD VPN tests, the IIMB engine was compared with FreeBSD's default OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) on Ryzen 5 5600 VMs: OpenVPN DCO AES-256-GCM async 10 vs 6.0 Gbps; ChaCha20-Poly1305 async 7.0 vs 4.10 Gbps; IPsec-ESP AES-128-GCM async 7.68 vs 4.46 Gbps. On the Netgate SG-8200 (Atom C3758), OpenVPN AES-256-GCM async was 2.50 vs 1.50 Gbps.
hardware: OpenSSL comparison: unnamed 'test host with AVX2'. VPN tests: AMD Ryzen 5 5600 (KVM/QEMU VMs running FreeBSD-CURRENT) and Netgate SG-8200 (Intel Atom C3758).
stars_or_usage: 339 stars; used as the software crypto backend in DPDK, Intel(R) QAT Engine, and FD.io
tradeoffs: Job-based multi-buffer API is a different programming model than OpenSSL's EVP interface (best throughput requires batching many buffers together); x86-64/AArch64 specific, hand-written per-ISA assembly; targets IPsec/packet-processing workloads rather than general-purpose drop-in crypto.
caveats: The only OpenSSL head-to-head is one sentence in a downstream user's (Netgate) paper. name: BLAKE3
baseline: SHA-256 and SHA3-256: the fastest of SUPERCOP's implementations, whose candidates include OpenSSL-backed ones. BLAKE2b is also compared. The project's own chart used OpenSSL 1.1.1d SHA-256/SHA3-256 and BLAKE2b via blake2b_simd.
workload: Single-core, long-message hashing throughput in cycles/byte. eBASH defines this as 1/16384 of the cycle difference between 18208-byte and 1824-byte messages, taking the median of many runs.
claimed_speedup: eBASH long-message medians on 'panther' (Intel Core i7-1165G7, Tiger Lake, SUPERCOP 20260831): BLAKE3 0.51 cycles/byte vs SHA-256 2.21 (~4.3x), SHA3-256 5.50 (~10.8x), BLAKE2b 2.99 (~5.9x). Ratios are derived from page data. Each figure is the fastest SUPERCOP implementation of that primitive, and the candidates include the OpenSSL-backed sha256/sha3256 implementations. At 1536-byte messages BLAKE3 (2.88 c/b) is slower than SHA-256 (2.34 c/b) on this SHA-NI CPU.

The eBASH implementation page lists the best build per implementation: crypto_hash/blake3/avx512 used clang -mcpu=native -O3 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE (Debian Clang 14.0.6); the sha256/openssl wrapper used gcc -march=native -mtune=native -O2 -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE and links the system OpenSSL (version not stated). The long-message table does not say which implementation or compiler produced each best figure.
hardware: eBASH 'panther': Intel Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, AVX-512 + SHA-NI, 2.8 GHz). Also eBASH 'hertz': AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4).
license: CC0-1.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
tradeoffs: Different digest from SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2 (not a bit-compatible drop-in); Merkle-tree construction parallelizes across threads and SIMD lanes; official optimized implementations in Rust and C; explicitly not recommended for password hashing.

name: j-lanes tree hashing mode and j-lanes SHA-256 (Gueron)
workload: SHA-256 hashing of single messages ranging 2KB-132KB, using a 4-lanes SIMD tree-hashing mode (j=4) on AVX, versus standard serial SHA-256
claimed_speedup: 4-lanes SHA-256 is 1.97-2.53x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1c for 2KB-128KB messages (Fig. 3: 13.27 vs 6.75 c/B at 2KB; 12.78 vs 5.05 c/B at 128KB). The abstract gives ~2 to ~2.5x. Against the fastest serial implementation (the authors' own n-SMS) it is 1.5-1.97x per the abstract and 1.55-2x per Sec. 3. At 8KB it is also faster than tree-mode BLAKE and Keccak (Fig. 4).
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3rd Gen Core, Ivy Bridge, AVX), with Hyper-Threading, Turbo Boost and Enhanced SpeedStep disabled
tradeoffs: Requires restructuring hashing into a tree mode (message split into j independent SIMD lanes, then combined), which changes the digest unless both hasher and verifier use the same mode; needs AVX; author was an Intel researcher and later pushed related multi-buffer techniques toward OpenSSL/ISA-L.
caveats: j-lanes SHA-256 is a different hash construction: a tree mode whose digest differs from standard SHA-256, and the paper itself says it would need distinct IVs if standardized. It is not a drop-in replacement for OpenSSL SHA-256. The 'fastest publicly available' comparator is the author's own n-SMS code. No compiler or flags are stated and no code is released. The results are from 2012 hardware against OpenSSL 1.0.1c, which predates OpenSSL's AVX2 and SHA-NI SHA-256 paths. The peer-reviewed venue is a SCIRP journal, a publisher whose review standards are widely questioned.

The abstract's '~6.73 c/B, almost 3x' figure is with the CPU down-clocked to 1.6GHz (UNIFORM: 6.73 vs 19.26 c/B, 2.86x).
hardware: Intel Core i5-2500 (Sandy Bridge, 3.3GHz; some disk runs down-clocked to 2.6/1.7/1.6GHz), Turbo Boost, Hyper-Threading and SpeedStep disabled, 8GB DDR3-1600, RAID0 of two Intel SSD 320, Fedora 16

caveats: Applies only when many independent messages are available: each message still gets a standard SHA-256 digest, but a single message is not sped up (see j-lanes for that). OpenSSL RT ticket 2784 is the authors' n-SMS patch (the faster serial comparator), not S-HASH itself. No S-HASH code is released and no compiler or flags are stated. name: Intel ISA-L Crypto (multi-buffer SHA)
baseline: The best-known single-buffer SHA-256 of 2012. The whitepaper cites Intel's own 'Fast SHA-256 Implementations on Intel Architecture Processors' (Guilford, Yap, Gopal, May 2012; ref [4]). OpenSSL is not named.
workload: Multi-Hash SHA-256 (SHA256x4) of a single 1 MB buffer on one core with Hyper-Threading and Turbo Boost off. SHA256x4 is a tree-mode extension that interleaves one buffer across 4 SIMD lanes and then hashes the lane digests, so its output is not a standard SHA-256 digest. Timing is rdtsc cycles/byte, using the trimmed mean of many runs.
claimed_speedup: ~5 cycles/byte for Multi-Hash SHA-256 on a 1 MB buffer, 'over 2X faster than the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' (Executive Summary). The Results section says SHA256x4 Multi-Hash gives a '~2.6X performance gain over the best SHA256 algorithm computation' at 1 MB, and MD5 Multi-Hash (x8) gives '~4.4X'.
hardware: Intel Core i7-2600 (Sandy Bridge), single core with Intel HT Technology, Turbo Boost off
tradeoffs: Only accelerates throughput when multiple independent buffers can be scheduled concurrently; needs application-level batching (not a transparent single-call speedup); requires NASM/gas for the hand-written SIMD kernels.
caveats: The only published performance source is Intel's own July 2012 Multi-Hash whitepaper, run on a Core i7-2600 that predates SHA-NI. Its baseline is Intel's best-known single-buffer SHA-256 code (ref [4]), not OpenSSL, and it states no compiler or flags. It measures Multi-Hash, a tree-mode SHA-256 variant whose digest is not interoperable with standard SHA-256, in a 4-lane (SHA256x4) layout. The shipped mh_sha256 uses 16 segments (ISAL_HASH_SEGS 16), so the paper's figures do not describe the current code. The library's standard-digest multi-buffer SHA-256 (sha256_mb) has no published numbers. The repo does ship OpenSSL head-to-head perf harnesses (sha256_mb/sha256_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c, sha1_mb/sha1_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c) but commits no results. No modern comparison against OpenSSL with SHA extensions was found.

claimed_speedup: Against Go crypto/sha256 (the README's 'golang' column), the ARM64 path on a 1.2GHz Cortex-A53 (Pine64) is 8.38x at 8B, 57.75x at 1KB, 95.11x at 8KB and 105.49x at 1MB (638.23 vs 6.05 MB/s). That Go version predates stdlib ARM64 SHA2 support. The x86 figures are package-internal: AVX512 3498.20 vs its own AVX2 path 448.62 MB/s (7.80x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.0GHz Xeon Platinum 8124M), and SHA Extensions 1975.17 vs its own AVX2 path 514.40 MB/s (3.84x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.7GHz Ryzen 7 2700X per the README Performance table).
hardware: 3.0 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX512); 3.7 GHz AMD Ryzen 7 2700X (SHA Extensions); 1.2 GHz ARM Cortex-A53 (Pine64). The Celeron J3455 is only named as a SHA-Ext-capable CPU, not as a benchmark host.

It was never benchmarked against modern stdlib SHA-NI. The x86 README numbers are against the package's own AVX2 path, not the stdlib. No commits since 2023-02-22 (about 3.6 years), so it is flagged abandoned.
